concept.name: Impermanent loss
concept.definition: Impermanent loss is the difference in value between depositing tokens into an AMM liquidity pool and simply holding those same tokens: as relative prices change, arbitrage rebalances the pool so the LP ends up with less of the appreciating asset and more of the depreciating one.
concept.intuition: The pool automatically sells your winners and buys your losers; if prices snap back the 'loss' vanishes — but if you withdraw while prices have diverged, it becomes real.
concept.mechanics: Under x·y=k, when the external price of one token rises, arbitrageurs buy it from the pool until the internal price matches, changing the reserve ratio. For a relative price change of factor r, IL = 2√r/(1+r) − 1 vs holding (e.g. r=2 → −5.7%, r=5 → −25.5%), independent of direction. Fees and incentives may or may not offset it.
concept.formula: IL(r) = 2√r / (1 + r) − 1, where r is the ratio of the new relative price to the price at deposit.
concept.failure_modes: IL grows non-linearly with divergence, so volatile or trending pairs can leave LPs deep underwater versus holding even after fees; concentrated liquidity amplifies IL per unit of capital when price leaves the range.
concept.misconceptions: 'Impermanent' does not mean harmless — the loss is permanent the moment you withdraw at a diverged price, and the original price often never returns. Fee income is not guaranteed to cover IL; for many pairs and periods it does not.
concept.example: Deposit 1 ETH + 1,000 USDC when ETH = $1,000 (pool: 10 ETH + 10,000 USDC, you own 10%). ETH doubles to $2,000; arbitrage leaves the pool at 7.071 ETH + 14,142 USDC. Your 10% withdrawal is worth $2,828 vs $3,000 for holding — a 5.7% impermanent loss.

citations.source: Chainlink - Understanding Impermanent Loss in DeFi Liquidity Pools
